nameStory: The hedgehog slug gets its spiky nickname from its defensive behavior when threatened. Just like a hedgehog curls into a protective ball, this slug contracts into a tight, rounded shape that makes it look almost like a tiny spiny creature. The "hedgehog" name captures this endearing habit of tucking in when danger approaches.
description: The hedgehog slug is a medium-sized land slug that belongs to the roundback slug family, known for their distinctively high, rounded body shape when at rest. These European natives have established themselves across New England, where they're often found in gardens and wooded areas. They typically reach about 2-3 inches when fully extended, with a smooth, moist body that can range from gray to brown in color. Like all slugs, they're essentially snails without shells, leaving behind telltale slime trails as they move.

idTips.label: Defensive posture
idTips.description: When disturbed, contracts into a tight, dome-shaped ball that feels firm to the touch and looks almost spiky or lumpy rather than smooth

idTips.label: Body shape at rest
idTips.description: Has a distinctively high, rounded back even when relaxed, giving it a humpbacked appearance unlike flatter slug species

idTips.label: Color pattern
idTips.description: Usually gray to brownish with a mottled or slightly banded appearance, often with a darker line running down the back

idTips.label: Size and texture
idTips.description: Medium-sized slug with smooth, very slimy skin that feels noticeably wet and slippery when touched

idTips.label: Breathing pore
idTips.description: Has a circular breathing hole (pneumostome) on the right side of its body that opens and closes rhythmically

habitat: Look for hedgehog slugs in moist, shaded areas throughout New England, particularly in deciduous and mixed forests with rich, organic soil. They're commonly found under logs, leaf litter, and stones, as well as in gardens where they feed on decaying plant matter and sometimes living plants. They prefer areas that stay consistently damp, such as stream edges, compost piles, and the north sides of buildings.

seasonality.spring: Most active as temperatures warm and moisture increases. Look for them emerging from winter hiding spots under logs and stones, often leaving fresh slime trails on damp mornings.
seasonality.summer: Active during humid periods and after rain, but may be harder to spot during dry spells when they retreat to deeper shelter. Early morning and evening are best viewing times.
seasonality.fall: Very active as they feed heavily before winter, often seen on fallen leaves and around decomposing organic matter. This is peak season for observation.
seasonality.winter: Largely inactive and hidden deep under logs, stones, or in soil. Occasionally spotted on unusually warm winter days, but generally dormant until spring.

funFact: Hedgehog slugs are hermaphrodites that can actually change their reproductive role mid-mating, with one partner sometimes literally stabbing the other with a calcium carbonate "love dart" to increase the chances of successful fertilization!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other Arion slugs, but the hedgehog slug's trademark defensive curl into a tight, almost spiky-looking ball is unique. Remember: "Hedgehog huddle" - when poked, it balls up just like its mammalian namesake, while other slugs just contract or stretch out.
contextualKnowledge: Like many slug species in New England, the hedgehog slug is actually a European native that arrived with human activity. Despite being non-native, they've become a naturalized part of our ecosystem and are generally not considered highly invasive, focusing mainly on decomposing organic matter rather than devastating live plants.
compareHints: Among its Arion relatives, the hedgehog slug is most distinctive for its defensive curling behavior - the Black Slug and Garden Arion don't ball up nearly as dramatically. The Western and Northern Dusky Slugs are typically smaller and lack the pronounced rounded back shape. The Orange-banded Arion has more obvious color banding, while the Darkface Arion has a characteristically dark head region that hedgehog slugs lack.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's Arion slugs, the Western Dusky Slug is one of the smallest and plainest-looking members of its genus.
Garden Arions are smaller and more compact than their relatives like the Black Slug, which can grow much larger and stays more elongated when disturbed.

Black Slugs are the largest and most robust of the Arion genus in New England, with that distinctive rounded back that sets them apart from their smaller, more elongated relatives like the Western Dusky Slug or Garden Arion.
Within the Arion genus, the Northern Dusky Slug is much smaller and more subdued in color compared to the large, jet-black Black Slug or the distinctively marked Orange-banded Arion.

Among its Arion relatives in New England, the Orange-banded Arion is the only one with prominent orange side bands - the Black Slug is uniformly dark, the Garden Arion is typically smaller and grayer, and the Dusky Slugs lack any bright coloration.

Among New England's Arion slugs, the Darkface Arion is most easily distinguished by its characteristic dark facial markings, while the Garden Arion tends to be more uniformly colored and the Black Slug is typically much larger and darker overall.
